IN THIS LESSON
The giraffe is the tallest living land animal, 14 to 19 feet tall; a newborn is about 6 feet tall (National Geographic Kids, 'Giraffe').
To drink water, a giraffe must spread its long legs outward and lower its head (National Geographic Kids, 'Giraffe').

Arctic foxes live on the Arctic tundra; their coat is white in winter and turns brown or gray in summer for camouflage (Britannica; Columbus Zoo).

title: Baby Animals for Kids! How Animal Babies Grow with Milo
description:
How do baby animals grow? Guess the baby with Milo the bluebird, then find out: bear cubs are born in a den in the middle of winter, a foal usually stands up within an hour of being born, and a baby elephant cannot drink with its trunk yet, so it kneels down, while the whole family helps look after it.
An interactive animal lesson for kids ages 2-6, with questions to answer, counting, actions to copy, quick checks and a quiz at the end.

The Animated Zoo makes gentle, colorful videos for little learners. New videos every day! Made with care for ages 2-6. Every fact is checked against trusted sources and every script is reviewed for kid safety before publishing.

IN THIS LESSON
Black bear cubs are born in the middle of the winter denning period (mid-January to early February), in their mothers' dens; they are born tiny, helpless and hairless, weighing less than half a pound, and stay with their mother for about 18 months; curved claws help black bears climb trees to search for food; 85% of a Great Smoky Mountains black bear's diet is berries and nuts (National Park Service, 'Black Bears', nps.gov/subjects/bears/black-bears.htm, read Nov 15 2026).
A newborn foal usually stands within 1 hour after birth, typically after several failed attempts; as soon as it is steady, often within an hour, it tries to nurse; it walks and runs for the first time within 90 minutes; by the end of the third month foals spend 60 percent of their time with other foals (eXtension Horses, 'Care of the newborn foal', horses.extension.org, read Nov 15 2026).
African savanna elephant calves weigh about 90-120 kg at birth and can stand about 15 minutes after birth; calves rely on milk only for the first 3 months; they cannot use the trunk to drink until about 8-9 months and get down on their knees to drink until they have enough trunk control; full trunk coordination at 1 year; calves are looked after by their mothers and other adult and subadult females in the herd, and the helpers let the mother feed and rest (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'African Elephants', Reproduction & Development, read Nov 15 2026).

description:
Super senses! Pick your answer with Milo the bluebird, then find out how three animals see, hear and smell: a hippo has its eyes, ears and nose on top of its head so it can peek out of the water, a rhino cannot see very well but hears and smells super well, and a fox can hear tiny animals digging under the snow.

IN THIS LESSON
Hippo eyes, ears and nostrils are on top of the head, so it can hear, see and breathe while most of its body is underwater (San Diego Zoo, zoo.sandiegozoo.org/animals/hippo); nostrils close before it goes under and the ears fold into a recess to close underwater (San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance Library fact sheet 'Hippopotamus', Physical Characteristics, read Nov 15 2026).
Mature hippos can stay under water for 5 minutes; hippos do not really swim, they move forward by punting off the river bottom; the herd leaves the water shortly before dark to graze (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Hippopotamus', Behavior & Ecology, read Nov 15 2026). Diet: grasses and other vegetation near rivers (same fact sheet, summary).
White rhino: poor eyesight, good sense of hearing, good sense of smell; the second largest land mammal, only surpassed in size by the elephant (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'White Rhinoceros', Physical Characteristics, read Nov 15 2026).
Rhino horn is made mainly of keratin, a protein also found in human hair and fingernails, and grows by around 2 cm each year (Save the Rhino International, 'What is rhino horn made of?', read Nov 15 2026).
Red foxes can hear the low-frequency sounds of small animals digging under the ground, leaves or snow; they stalk and pounce on prey; the tail is used for balance, warmth and signaling; adults have a dozen calls; young are called kits (Missouri Department of Conservation, 'What Red Foxes Say and Do', read Nov 15 2026).

title: What Do Animals Eat? Bamboo, Leaves and Grass
description:
What do animals eat? Pick your answer with Milo the bluebird, then find out: a panda's food is almost all bamboo and it grips the stems with a special thumb-like bump, a koala eats almost only eucalyptus leaves and sniffs out its favorites, and a zebra snips grass with its front teeth and can drink more than a gallon of water at one time.
An interactive animal lesson for kids ages 2-6, with questions to answer, counting, actions to copy, quick checks and a quiz at the end.

The Animated Zoo makes gentle, colorful videos for little learners. New videos every day! Made with care for ages 2-6. Every fact is checked against trusted sources and every script is reviewed for kid safety before publishing.

IN THIS LESSON
At least 98% of a giant panda's diet is bamboo; active for roughly 14 hours per day, spending most of this time foraging; grasps bamboo with the front feet, between palm and thumb-like digit (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Giant Panda', Diet & Feeding, ielc.libguides.com/sdzg/factsheets/giantpanda/diet, read Nov 16 2026).
Giant panda: unique thumb-like digit (modified sesamoid bone), enlarged and covered in a tough pad; large, flat molars for grinding bamboo; strong jaw bones and chewing muscles give a bite force higher than any other bear (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Giant Panda', Physical Characteristics, read Nov 16 2026).
Koalas feed almost exclusively on leaves of Eucalyptus; smell plays a role in identifying preferred species; koalas rarely drink in the wild and produce dry pellets (water conservation) (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Koala', Diet & Feeding, read Nov 16 2026).
An adult koala spends about 19-20 hours a day sitting or sleeping; a low-energy lifestyle is necessary for an animal that specializes on such a low-energy diet (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Koala', Behavior & Ecology, read Nov 16 2026).
Plains zebras primarily consume grasses (more than 90% of diet), about 50 grass species; incisor teeth crop grasses, cheek teeth grind the food; they immerse their lips below the water surface to drink and may take in more than 4 liters (1 gallon) in a single bout (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Plains Zebra', Diet & Feeding, read Nov 16 2026).
Plains zebras form large herds of several hundred; social grooming: they clean one another's coat and mane (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Plains Zebra', Behavior & Ecology, read Nov 16 2026).

title: Amazing Animal Feet! Paws, Claws and Toes for Kids
description:
Whose feet are these? Pick your answer with Milo the bluebird, then look closely: a polar bear has wide feet like paddles with tiny bumps that help it grip the ice, a tiger can pull its long claws in and out and can swim across big rivers, and a hippo spreads its four toes wide to walk on the soft river bottom.

IN THIS LESSON
Polar bear: wide, large, paddle-like feet; 5 toes on each foot; claws non-retractable, 5-7 cm long; soles of feet have small dermal bumps (papillae) that may help with traction on ice; even foot pads are furred in winter; covered with fur except for the nose; 5-10 cm of fat, and both fat and pelt provide insulation (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Polar Bear', Physical Characteristics, ielc.libguides.com/sdzg/factsheets/polarbear/characteristics, read Nov 16 2026).

Tigers can cross rivers 6-8 km (4-5 mi) wide (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Tiger', Behavior & Ecology, read Nov 16 2026).
Hippo: four functional toes with wide splay; nail-like hooves on the ends of the toes; partial webbing on the feet; being able to splay the digits is a good adaptation for walking in water on soft river bottoms; mucous glands secrete a thick, oily red fluid that dries like lacquer and protects the thin skin against water loss, sunburn and infection (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Hippopotamus', Physical Characteristics, read Nov 16 2026).

IN THIS LESSON
African elephant: large ear surface area with networks of vessels close to the skin surface allow heat to leave the body; flapping the ears dissipates a lot of body heat; wrinkles help the skin retain moisture, and water and mud adhere to wrinkly skin, which boosts evaporative cooling; elephants spray dust, grass and water on the body; they walk on tiptoes with large fat pads cushioning the feet; they may detect vibrations through their feet (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'African Elephants', Physical Characteristics, ielc.libguides.com/sdzg/factsheets/african_elephant/characteristics, read Nov 16 2026).
Koala: posture changes help with body temperature regulation; on hot days they extend their limbs, and in cold, wet, windy weather they fold their arms and legs in; arboreal, but must travel on the ground to move to another tree; males produce low-frequency bellows; koalas spend most of their time alone (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Koala', Behavior & Ecology, read Nov 16 2026).
Tiger: larger subspecies often regulate body temperature by lying partially submerged in shaded pools; active both day and night; sounds include grunting, miaowing, woofing, growling, hissing and prusten or chuffing (gentle puffing); both sexes scent-mark their territories (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'Tiger', Behavior & Ecology, read Nov 16 2026). White rhino: two horns on the rostrum, one in front of the other; composed of keratin (not true horns); grow continually throughout life; upper lip broad, flat, specialized to help secure grass; poor eyesight; good sense of smell; second-largest land mammal, only surpassed in size by elephant; skin very thick with deep folds (SDZWA Library fact sheet 'White Rhinoceros', Physical Characteristics, ielc.libguides.com/sdzg/factsheets/whiterhino/characteristics, read Nov 17 2026).
